title: Observability
subtitle: Watch a slow database turn into a page for the on-call engineer, and see which signal answers which question.
learn: How metrics, logs, and traces differ and what question each one answers
How the RED and USE methods pick which numbers to watch
How a trace ID ties one request together across services
Why you page on symptoms users feel, not on causes like CPU

steps.title: Is checkout healthy right now?
steps.body: A checkout system handles about 400 requests per second. It works today, but at 2 a.m. something will break and nobody will be watching. You usually cannot attach a debugger to production, so the only way to know what happened is what the system recorded about itself. Observability is how well you can answer new questions about a running system from its outputs.
steps.idea: You cannot fix what you cannot see, and in production the only thing you can see is what the system emitted.
steps.caption: A healthy baseline: 400 req/s, 0.1% errors, p99 of 220 ms.

steps.title: Three signals, three questions
steps.body: Each service sends telemetry to a collector. Metrics are numbers over time, such as requests per second: cheap, and good for "is something wrong?". Logs are timestamped event records: detailed, and good for "what exactly happened?". Traces follow one request across services: good for "where did the time go?". No single signal answers all three.
steps.idea: Metrics tell you that something is wrong, traces tell you where, and logs tell you why.
steps.caption: Services push metrics, logs, and spans to a collector.

steps.title: Metrics: RED for services, USE for resources
steps.body: Services are instrumented with a library such as OpenTelemetry, and a collector (for example the OpenTelemetry Collector) forwards metrics to the metrics store, which keeps them as time series, sampled every 15 seconds or so. For anything that serves requests, watch RED: Rate (requests per second), Errors (share that fail), and Duration (latency, as percentiles like p99 (the latency 99% of requests beat), not averages). For resources such as a database host or queue, watch USE: Utilization, Saturation (work waiting), and Errors. Keep labels low in variety: a user_id label creates millions of series and makes storage and queries very costly.
steps.idea: RED asks how users are served; USE asks how machines are coping. Avoid high-cardinality labels.
steps.caption: Aggregated numbers land in the metrics store.

steps.title: Logs: detailed, but expensive
steps.body: Each service also writes one structured JSON line per event: timestamp, level, order id, and the trace ID. Structured fields can be searched and filtered, unlike free text. The cost adds up. At about 2 KB of logs per request and 400 requests per second, that is roughly 70 GB a day, so teams log at the right level and sample noisy debug lines.
steps.idea: Log structured events with a trace ID, and budget for volume, since it grows with traffic.
steps.caption: Structured log lines flow to the logs store.

steps.title: Traces: one ID across every hop
steps.body: The Checkout API creates a trace ID for the incoming request and passes it to every downstream call in a header (the W3C traceparent standard). Each service records a span: its name, start time, duration, and parent span. Spans that share a trace ID assemble into one timeline of the whole request (the ID 4bf9 is shown shortened; real IDs are 32 hex characters, and an instrumented client can start the trace instead). Tracing every request is costly, so teams sample. Sampling up front (say 1%) is cheap but can miss the bad request; sampling after the trace finishes lets you keep every slow or failed one.
steps.idea: A propagated trace ID turns separate service logs into one story per request.
steps.caption: The trace ID travels with the request; spans go to the collector.

steps.title: The database slows down
steps.body: A batch update runs in one long transaction and holds row locks in the orders database. Most writes still take about 20 ms, but those that wait on a locked row now take over 2 seconds, and about 5% wait past the payment call's 3 second timeout and fail. Nothing crashed, no server is down, and CPU looks fine. From the user's side, checkout is slow and 4.8% of attempts fail.
steps.idea: Many real outages are slowness, not crashes, so you must measure latency and errors, not just uptime.
steps.caption: The database answers slowly; payments time out.

steps.title: Page on symptoms, not causes
steps.body: An alert rule reads the metrics store and pages a human only for something users feel, such as "checkout errors above 2% for 5 minutes". Alerting on causes like "CPU above 80%" fires on harmless spikes and stays silent on this lock problem. A good version uses SLO burn rate. An SLO is a reliability target; a 99.9% target leaves an error budget of 0.1% failures, and burn rate is how many times faster than budgeted you are spending it. Here 4.8% errors burns the budget about 48 times too fast. Causes mostly belong on dashboards, not on pagers, unless they predict imminent user impact (for example, disk full within hours).
steps.idea: Every page should mean users are hurting and a human must act now; everything else is a dashboard or a ticket.
steps.caption: The rule fires and one page reaches the on-call engineer.

steps.title: From symptom to cause
steps.body: Paged at 2 a.m., the engineer opens the dashboard, which shows RED going bad: errors up and p99 up at the Checkout API, with rate unchanged. That locates the problem but not the cause. Opening a slow but successful trace shows a 2.1 second span inside the orders database call, and the log lines with that trace ID reveal lock waits. USE on the database confirms it: saturation is high while CPU is low.
steps.idea: Work top-down: a metric finds the symptom, a trace finds the slow hop, a log explains it.
steps.caption: Metrics point to the symptom; traces and logs find the cause.

steps.title: See, locate, explain, wake someone
steps.body: Metrics show that users are hurting, using RED for services and USE for resources. Traces carrying one ID show which hop is slow, and structured logs explain why. Alerts watch user-facing symptoms so a page means real impact. Instrument before you need it: the outage you cannot see is the one you cannot fix.
steps.idea: Metrics detect, traces locate, logs explain, and symptom-based alerts decide who gets woken up.
steps.caption: The full path from request to telemetry to a page.

quiz.q: Checkout p99 latency tripled but traffic and error rate are normal. Which signal best tells you which downstream call is responsible?
options: A CPU utilization graph for the API servers
A distributed trace of a slow request
A count of total requests per minute
The service's uptime percentage
quiz.why: A trace breaks one slow request into spans per hop, so you can see which call ate the time. Rate and uptime would look normal here.

quiz.q: You are monitoring a message queue. Which set matches the USE method?
options: Rate, Errors, Duration
Uptime, Speed, Errors
Latency, Traffic, Capacity
Utilization, Saturation, Errors
quiz.why: USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) is for resources like queues and disks. RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is for request-serving services.

quiz.q: Which alert is the better page for the on-call engineer?
options: Database CPU above 80% for 1 minute
Disk usage above 60%
Checkout success rate below 98% for 5 minutes
A single pod restarted
quiz.why: It measures what users experience and needs action. The others are possible causes that often fire harmlessly, so they belong on dashboards or tickets.

quiz.q: Should you add a user_id label to every metric time series?
options: No, because each distinct value creates a new series and cost explodes
Yes, because it lets you filter any metric by user
Yes, because metrics are free to store
No, because labels slow down the network
quiz.why: Each unique label combination is its own time series. Unbounded values like user IDs create millions of series. Put such detail in logs or traces instead.

quiz.q: Checkout requests succeed normally, but a trace shows only the Checkout API span, with no spans from the Payments service. What is the most likely cause?
options: Payments is down
The database is too slow
The trace ID header was not passed on the call to Payments
Metrics are being sampled too often
quiz.why: If the trace context header is dropped, Payments starts its own unconnected trace. Propagating the ID on every outbound call is what stitches spans together.

cheatsheet.def: Numbers sampled over time. Cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts, but they hide the detail of individual requests.
Timestamped event records. Use structured JSON with a trace ID so they can be searched and joined to traces.
A trace is one request's whole journey; a span is one timed step inside it. The trace ID travels in headers such as W3C traceparent so every service joins the same trace.
For services: Rate, Errors, Duration. Use percentiles such as p99 for duration, not averages.
For resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Saturation (queued work) often shows trouble before utilization does.
The number of distinct label combinations on a metric. Unbounded labels like user_id blow up storage and cost.
An SLO is a reliability target, such as 99.9% success. Its error budget is the allowed 0.1% failures; burn rate is how many times faster than budgeted you are spending it.
Page on user-visible impact (errors, latency, SLO burn rate). Keep cause metrics like CPU on dashboards.
